newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mobil concerned as Nigeria renegotiates MOU.
newsitem.headline: Mobil concerned as Nigeria renegotiates MOU.

text.p: Mobil Corp said on Tuesday it was concerned that renegotiation of the oil industry's Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Nigerian government could undermine investor confidence in the country.

Victor Oyofo, production manager for Mobil Nigeria, told the Africa Oil conference that the introduction of the first MOU in the 1980s, in response to falling production, had been a great success in providing greater certainty to investors.
But there was a danger that the benefits of this could now be squandered.
"As it stands today, the MOU which was a greater incentive for people to produce and deliver has been eroded," he said.
"If there are written rules...investors need the comfort that the rules that they base their investment on do not materially change."
The MOU as amended in 1991 is currently being renegotiated and revised after a five year term. Oil companies are anxious to ensure reasonable margins.

Relations between the government and foreign oil companies came under strain at the end of August when Oil Minister Dan Etete announced strict new rules for firms which the government said were short-changing the country.
The new rules required joint ventures to set up escrow accounts, allowing the government to keep a closer eye on where contributions to production and exploration costs were going.

They also required oil industry service contracts to be awarded to locally-registered companies and allowed the government to hand over undeveloped marginal oil fields to those who are "seriously interested in exploiting them".

State-run Nigerian National Petroleum Corp is in joint ventures with subsidiaries of six major exploration and production operators -- Royal Dutch/Shell, Mobil Corp, Chevron Corp, Texaco, Agip SpA and Elf Aquitaine.
